chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ayyar, who said:

A woman from my family bequeathed to me one-third of her wealth and ordered that it be used to free a slave, perform Hajj, and give charity. When this amount was not sufficient to cover all three, I asked Abu Hanifa about it, and he said: 'It should be divided into three parts: one-third for manumission, one-third for Hajj, and one-third for charity.'

So I went to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said to him: 'Indeed, a woman from my family died and bequeathed to me one-third of her wealth, ordering that a slave be freed on her behalf, charity be given, and Hajj be performed on her behalf. I looked into it, but the amount was not sufficient.'
He said: 'Begin with Hajj, for it is a duty among the duties of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. And whatever remains should be set aside as a portion for charity.'
So I informed Abu Hanifa of the saying of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he returned from his opinion and adopted the opinion of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).
ai.seo_question: How should a limited bequest be distributed when it must cover Hajj, manumission, and charity?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights a key jurisprudential difference between the Shia Imams and the Sunni school regarding the prioritization of bequests when funds are insufficient. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a hierarchy by prioritizing Hajj as a fundamental divine obligation (*fard*) over manumission and charity, a ruling that led Abu Hanifa to adopt the Imam's view. This emphasizes the Shia principle that fulfilling obligatory acts takes precedence over voluntary or secondary bequests in estate distribution.
